<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Aashiq Muhamed
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Correspondence to <span id="id1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">amuhamed@cs.cmu.edu</span>.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mona T. Diab
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Virginia Smith
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Carnegie Mellon University
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Safety guardrails in open-weight language models can be readily bypassed using Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA), a technique that identifies and projects out a linear <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusal direction</em> from the residual stream, often achieving a high attack success rate (ASR) while preserving model capability. Defending against these attacks typically requires computationally expensive safety finetuning for every new checkpoint. We introduce <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO)</span>, a fast, post-hoc weight-editing defense that requires no base-model finetuning. Our approach is based on a simple mechanistic insight: ablation attacks rely on contrastive estimators to find the refusal direction. Rather than trying to hide the true refusal circuitry, DDO actively injects a high-magnitude, nonlinear <em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">decoy</em> signal into the network’s MLP neurons. When an attacker attempts to locate the refusal direction, the decoy corrupts their estimator, tricking them into ablating a harmless orthogonal feature while the actual safety mechanism remains intact. We prove a spectral bound formalizing this effect and evaluate DDO across six model families, achieving <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>10% ASR under standard RFA. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DDO remains comparable to trained defenses under adaptive multi-phase attacks (<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>65</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="58\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>58</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">58\%</annotation></semantics></math> worst-case ASR) and reduces Heretic weight-level attack ASR from <math id="abstract1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="88.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>88.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">88.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="abstract1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\%</annotation></semantics></math>, all at <math id="abstract1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower optimization cost per configuration than the trained baselines.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
        Code: <a href="https://github.com/aashiqmuhamed/defending-against-abliteration" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/aashiqmuhamed/defending-against-abliteration</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ability to decline harmful requests is a core safety mechanism in instruction-tuned LLMs aligned via preference finetuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Removing refusal from open-weight models can fuel misuse, increasing risks such as chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) capability uplift; cyber-offense generation; and the production of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), making refusal robustness a pressing safety concern <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. In the open-weight setting, however, safety is brittle: a white-box adversary can modify the released checkpoint and its inference code, yielding a model that preserves capability while dropping refusal. Prior work suggests that refusal is often mediated by low-dimensional residual-stream features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, enabling training-free attacks such as Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA; also referred to as <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">abliteration</span>) that estimate a difference-in-means (DIM) direction between harmful and safe activations and project it out at inference time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. The resulting checkpoints often achieve high <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attack success rate</em> (ASR; harmful prompts judged compliant), and thousands of such uncensored variants are already publicly hosted <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.16204v1/comparison_figure.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/223;" width="476" height="223" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DDO vs. existing defenses against RFA.</span> Without any defense, RFA strips refusal from open-weight models with no training cost for the attacker (top row). Trained safety defenses (Circuit Breakers, LAT, ReFAT, RepBend) preserve refusal under RFA but require training data, multi-GPU finetuning, and expensive per-method hyperparameter sweeps (middle row). DDO reaches comparable standard-RFA robustness at <math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower cost: a single GPU, two minutes, no training data, and base weights left frozen (bottom row).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing defenses against refusal removal are predominantly training-time interventions. Circuit Breakers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> finetunes checkpoints with a representation-rerouting objective; LAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and ReFAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> adversarially train against latent/feature-space attacks; and RepBend <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and Triplet-based objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> reshape representation geometry during training. These methods can be highly effective, but they require safety finetuning and must be repeated for each new checkpoint. Depending on the method, they may additionally require method-specific training data or attack pipelines (e.g., adversarial examples) and hyperparameter tuning. Moreover, prior work does not evaluate these defenses against adaptive multi-phase RFA or automated weight-level attacks like Heretic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>; we evaluate under this stronger attack ladder (Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>). Given the rapid release cadence of open-weight checkpoints, and evidence that frontier open-weight models can trail closed-weight state-of-the-art on the order of months on capability benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, per-checkpoint retraining is difficult to sustain; we therefore seek <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-hoc</em> safety hardening tools that are low-cost, composable, and data-light.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO)</span>, a post-hoc defense that targets the attacker’s estimator rather than the refusal feature itself, without requiring expensive finetuning. DDO repurposes low-impact MLP neurons to implement a gated read–write map: on harmful prompts, the neurons <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">read</em> the refusal coordinate and <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">write</em> large updates in directions orthogonal to refusal, inducing a decoy-dominated contrast that biases DIM estimation so that RFA ablates a decoy signal rather than the causal refusal subspace. We prove a subspace overlap bound and specialize it to orthogonal decoys (Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Overlap bound under orthogonal decoys). ‣ Decoy contrast decomposition. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>): sufficiently strong decoy modes limit how much a contrastive attack overlaps the causal refusal subspace. The number of such modes defines an <em id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">effective decoy rank</em>, which also serves as a diagnostic for interpreting adaptive re-estimation budgets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, DDO is able to lower the ASR of standard-RFA to <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">less than <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math></span> on <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">six model families</span> in <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}2</annotation></semantics></math> minutes per optimization run on a single A100 GPU. DDO matches or exceeds trained baselines on standard RFA at <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> lower cost per configuration</span> (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, under adaptive multi-phase RFA, DDO degrades comparably to trained defenses (<math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>65</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65\%</annotation></semantics></math> worst-case ASR vs. <math id="S1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="58\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>58</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">58\%</annotation></semantics></math> for the best trained baseline) while preserving coherent generation (MT-Bench <math id="S1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq 5.82" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mn>5.82</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq 5.82</annotation></semantics></math>), and reduces Heretic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> ASR from <math id="S1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="88.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>88.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">88.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\%</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>200</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200</annotation></semantics></math> trials. Our contributions include:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(i)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DDO (Decoy Direction Optimization)</span>, to our knowledge, the first post-hoc defense against refusal feature ablation that requires no base-model finetuning. DDO repurposes a small set of <em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low-impact</em> MLP neurons to inject gated, refusal-orthogonal decoy directions that corrupt contrastive refusal estimators. The defense compiles into weights, incurring no architectural or runtime overhead.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(ii)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We prove <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">subspace overlap bounds</span> (Theorems <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Subspace overlap bound). ‣ Spectral analysis of contrastive ablation. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Overlap bound under orthogonal decoys). ‣ Decoy contrast decomposition. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) that relate attacker–refusal overlap to the contrast matrix and, for DDO, the spectrum of its empirical decoy response matrix. The resulting effective decoy rank characterizes protection against a fixed contrastive attack and helps interpret adaptive phase budgets. A corollary on optimal spectral allocation (Corollary <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 3 (Optimal spectrum under an energy constraint). ‣ Decoy energy allocation. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) provides a concrete design principle for multi-direction decoys: under a fixed decoy-energy budget, spreading energy evenly across <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> directions maximizes the <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th singular value, strengthening guarantees against rank-<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> contrastive ablation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(iii)</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a broad evaluation under a three-tier <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">training-free attack ladder</span> (standard RFA, adaptive multi-phase RFA, and Heretic), including head-to-head comparisons with trained defenses and cross-architecture mechanism ablations. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, DDO reduces standard-RFA ASR from <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> while preserving benign compliance, performing comparably to the strongest trained baselines at <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower cost per configuration. Across <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">six model families</span>, DDO achieves <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;10\%</annotation></semantics></math> standard-RFA ASR without base-model finetuning.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Related work.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the rank-1 refusal feature attack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>, recent work shows that refusal geometry can be multi-dimensional, e.g., concept cones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, multiple mediating directions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, orthogonal safety dimensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, and separable harmfulness/refusal representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, motivating our multi-phase adaptive attack evaluation. Prior model-level defenses against RFA require per-checkpoint safety finetuning with task-specific data and full backward passes through the model; DDO instead freezes all base weights and optimizes only a small set of decoy parameters, enabling post-hoc hardening in minutes with no inference-time overhead. We additionally evaluate prompt-level jailbreaks (GCG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, PAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, AutoDAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>), which have been linked to the same refusal features exploited by RFA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. Extended related work is in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Extended Related Work ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Threat Model and Attacks</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study refusal robustness in the open-weight release setting: a defender applies DDO to a checkpoint and releases only the hardened model; an adversary then obtains the defended weights and attempts to remove refusal while preserving general capability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our threat model targets the automated, training-free uncensoring pipeline that dominates open-weight model tampering. The low-barrier route is not safety unlearning or adversarial finetuning, but applying public <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">abliteration</span> or weight-editing tools to a released checkpoint. We model a <em id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">resource-constrained, white-box, and adaptive</em> attacker who can inspect released weights, run arbitrary inference code, collect activations on harmful and benign probe prompts, modify activations at inference time, and apply post-hoc weight edits. Following Kerckhoffs’s principle, the attacker knows DDO was applied and can adapt their scripts accordingly, but has no access to the original pre-DDO checkpoint and does not perform gradient-based finetuning.
This captures the platform-side risk DDO addresses: a model provider, hosting platform, or downstream distributor may harden a checkpoint before release, but cannot assume downstream users will not attempt to strip safety guardrails.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The attacker’s objective is <em id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">capability-preserving refusal removal</em>: maximize ASR on harmful prompts while preserving coherent generation. Since ASR can be artificially lowered by destroying model quality, we evaluate robustness jointly with utility metrics (MT-Bench, MMLU, XSTest).
We operationalize this threat model with three tiers of training-free attacks (Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Standard RFA. ‣ 2 Threat Model and Attacks ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), forming a ladder of increasing attacker sophistication within the post-hoc, no-finetuning regime.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Standard RFA.</h4>

<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Attack surface by tier. The three tiers probe complementary attack channels.</figcaption>

<td id="S2.T1.2.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S2.T1.2.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F5F5F5;">✓</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The attacker estimates a per-layer difference-in-means (DIM) direction and projects it out of the residual stream <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. Let <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the residual stream at layer <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>. The attacker computes</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\mid\mathrm{harm}]-\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\mid\mathrm{safe}],\qquad\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\ell}}{\|\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\|_{2}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>harm</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>safe</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\mid\mathrm{harm}]-\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\mid\mathrm{safe}],\qquad\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\frac{\mathbf{d}_{\ell}}{\|\mathbf{d}_{\ell}\|_{2}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">for nonzero <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{d}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐝</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{d}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, and applies <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\leftarrow(\mathbf{I}-\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{\top})\mathbf{h}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\leftarrow(\mathbf{I}-\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{\top})\mathbf{h}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. We reserve <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> for the defender’s reference refusal direction and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> for the attacker’s estimate on the released model. We evaluate both <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">three-point</em> and <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">residual-stream</em> variants (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Attack Implementation Details ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>) on JailbreakBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> and HarmBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Heretic.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Heretic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> is a fully automated weight-level refusal-removal tool that applies Optuna-optimized <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> low-rank projections to attention output <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> and MLP down-projection <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{ablated}}=\mathbf{W}-\alpha(\ell)\,\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\hat{\mathbf{d}}^{\top}\mathbf{W})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>ablated</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{ablated}}=\mathbf{W}-\alpha(\ell)\,\hat{\mathbf{d}}(\hat{\mathbf{d}}^{\top}\mathbf{W})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a searched ablation direction and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha(\ell)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha(\ell)</annotation></semantics></math> is a searched per-layer ablation strength. It produces a modified checkpoint and requires no ML expertise. We report H-200 as the maximum-ASR trial among 200 Optuna trials (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Attack Implementation Details ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Adaptive multi-phase RFA.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To model an attacker who adapts after observing the defended checkpoint, we introduce an iterative variant. At phase <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the attacker computes a fresh DIM vector <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐝</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> with all earlier phases’ ablations active, then removes its components along previously selected directions:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}=\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)}-\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\langle\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(j)}\rangle\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(j)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(t)}=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}\|_{2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}=\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)}-\sum_{j=1}^{t-1}\langle\mathbf{d}_{\ell}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(j)}\rangle\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(j)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(t)}=\frac{\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}\|_{2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The sum is empty at <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math>. Normalization applies when <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}\neq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐯</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\ell}^{(t)}\neq 0</annotation></semantics></math>; otherwise we set <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(t)}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\ell}^{(t)}=0</annotation></semantics></math> and add no new direction. The attacker ablates all accumulated directions simultaneously, giving rank at most <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> per layer. Throughout, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> indexes adaptive phases, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> denotes attack rank, and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of decoy reader groups.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO)</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider standard pre-norm decoder-only transformers with SwiGLU/GeGLU MLPs (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Notation and Background ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>). Let <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the residual-stream state at layer <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>attn</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the residual stream after the attention update (before the MLP). The MLP input is <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>RMSNorm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>attn</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}})</annotation></semantics></math>. SwiGLU uses gate/up projections <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{inter}}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>inter</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{inter}}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> and down projection <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{inter}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>inter</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{inter}}}</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{inter}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>inter</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{inter}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the MLP intermediate dimension and <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{silu}(x)=x\sigma(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>silu</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{silu}(x)=x\sigma(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the SiLU activation) to produce the residual update <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{m}_{\ell}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\!\big(\operatorname{silu}(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell})\odot(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell})\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐦</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>silu</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{m}_{\ell}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\!\big(\operatorname{silu}(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell})\odot(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell})\big)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math> is elementwise multiplication. DDO operates by editing select rows/columns of <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO)</span> is a post-hoc weight-editing defense (base weights frozen) that targets the attacker’s contrastive estimator rather than the refusal feature. On harmful prompts, DDO repurposes a small number of SwiGLU/GeGLU neurons to inject large residual shifts along decoy directions orthogonal to refusal, so RFA’s estimated ablation direction becomes decoy-dominated, and ablation preferentially removes decoys rather than the underlying causal refusal subspace. All edits are folded into the deployed weights, incurring no additional architectural or runtime overhead. Concretely, DDO: (i) <span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">estimates</span> a per-layer refusal direction <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> via DIM on 128 harmful and 128 safe probes; (ii) <span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">selects</span> <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> low-impact neurons per target layer (smallest-norm columns of <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math>); (iii) <span id="S3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimizes</span> decoy write directions <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{i}\perp\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⟂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{i}\perp\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> under a four-term loss, tuning scalar gains <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta,s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\beta,s)</annotation></semantics></math> via Bayesian hyperparameter search; and (iv) <span id="S3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">compiles</span> the optimized parameters into weights using replace or additive mode, and places the edits at or upstream of the causal refusal zone.
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides a schematic of the DDO architecture, optimization objective, and geometric intuition.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2609.16204v1/ddo_method.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/201;" width="476" height="201"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>DDO overview. <span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A)</span> Gated decoy architecture: SwiGLU MLP neuron repurposing writes <math id="S3.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="S3.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}/\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}/\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}</annotation></semantics></math> (trigger) and <math id="S3.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{i}\perp\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⟂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{i}\perp\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> into <math id="S3.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math> (decoy output); gating <math id="S3.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{silu}(\beta a)\cdot a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>silu</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{silu}(\beta a)\cdot a</annotation></semantics></math> produces harmful-selective shifts. <span id="S3.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(B)</span> DDO optimizes <math id="S3.F2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{u}_{i}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{u}_{i}\}</annotation></semantics></math> via four losses: refusal preservation, benign retention, estimator confusion, and first-token anchoring (with <math id="S3.F2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta,s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta,s</annotation></semantics></math> tuned by Optuna). <span id="S3.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(C)</span> The defended mean-difference <math id="S3.F2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\text{def}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>def</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\text{def}}</annotation></semantics></math> rotates toward the decoy subspace; ablating it removes decoys but preserves true refusal <math id="S3.F2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Gated decoy architecture.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DDO repurposes a small set of SwiGLU (or GeGLU) units to implement a gated read–write map: each unit <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">reads</em> the refusal coordinate and <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">writes</em> into an orthogonal decoy direction. To minimize utility loss, we choose <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low-impact</em> units per layer by selecting the <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> smallest-norm columns of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math> (units whose down-projection contributes weakly to the residual update). In each targeted layer <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and for each selected unit <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we write a refusal-aligned trigger into row <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}}</annotation></semantics></math> (denoted <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{up},i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>up</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{up},i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate},i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>gate</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate},i}</annotation></semantics></math>), and a decoy write vector into column <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}</annotation></semantics></math> (denoted <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{down},i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>down</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{down},i}</annotation></semantics></math>):</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{up},i}\leftarrow\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate},i}\leftarrow\beta\,\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{down},i}\leftarrow s\cdot\mathbf{u}_{i}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>up</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>gate</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐰</mi><mrow><mi>down</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{up},i}\leftarrow\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate},i}\leftarrow\beta\,\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell}^{\top},\quad\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{down},i}\leftarrow s\cdot\mathbf{u}_{i},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
