<td id="S4.T3.10.31.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T3.10.31.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">90.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.10.31.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T3.10.31.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">0.3</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.10.31.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T3.10.31.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">2.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.10.31.8" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><math id="S4.T3.m34" class="ltx_Math" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;" alttext="{\sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;" mathbackground="#E3F2FD" mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.T3.10.31.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">2m</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Across all six models, DDO achieves <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;10\%</annotation></semantics></math> mean standard-RFA ASR without base-model finetuning. On Qwen3 and GLM-4, DDO achieves the lowest RFA ASR among utility-preserving defenses. On Gemma-2, DDO matches LAT’s <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> RFA while preserving higher benign compliance (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="83.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>83.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">83.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="51.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>51.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">51.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> XSTest). DDO also reduces DirectRequest compliance on models with weaker native refusal (Yi: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="27\%\rightarrow 5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>27</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">27\%\rightarrow 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>; Mistral: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41\%\rightarrow 6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>41</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41\%\rightarrow 6\%</annotation></semantics></math>; GLM-4: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="26\%\rightarrow 0.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>26</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mn>0.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">26\%\rightarrow 0.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>). Beyond these six families, DDO transfers to seven additional models with per-model Optuna tuning (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}</annotation></semantics></math>10 min each), achieving <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>10% ASR on all of them (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS15" title="F.15 Additional Model Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.15</span></a>). A DDO optimization run takes <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}2</annotation></semantics></math> minutes on a single A100 GPU, giving a <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m11" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> per-configuration cost advantage over trained baselines (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\text{--}15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\text{--}15</annotation></semantics></math> A100-hours each).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compile-mode selection.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each model, we sweep both compile modes (replace and additive) with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>15</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15</annotation></semantics></math> Optuna trials per mode (Table <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ F.4 Compile Mode Selection Details ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>; Appendix Table <a href="#A6.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ F.6 Per-Model DDO Best Configs ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>). Replace mode overwrites the neuron’s original weights with the decoy, producing a stronger signal but removing the neuron’s original computation; additive mode superposes the decoy on top, preserving the original behavior at the cost of a weaker decoy. The preferred mode depends on how each model’s refusal circuitry responds to neuron overwriting: replace is preferred on Yi, Llama-3, and GLM-4 (where the model compensates for the lost neuron), while additive is preferred on Gemma-2 (replace fails the coherence check), Qwen3, and Mistral (replace disrupts baseline refusal). See Appendix <a href="#A6.SS4" title="F.4 Compile Mode Selection Details ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.4</span></a> for a detailed analysis.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Prompt-level jailbreak ASR (%<math id="S4.T4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>, 3-judge avg, HarmBench). HJB = HumanJailbreaks; ADAN = AutoDAN. <span id="S4.T4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">best</span> / <span id="S4.T4.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">good</span> / <span id="S4.T4.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFCDD2;">poor</span> / <span id="S4.T4.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">ours</span>. DDO + debiasing matches the best trained defenses on GCG (0.4%); PAIR remains high (36.3%).</figcaption>

<td id="S4.T4.10.9.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.9.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">1.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.9.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.9.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">1.7</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.10.9.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">37.5</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.9.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">0.0</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.10.10" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">
<th id="S4.T4.10.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">+debias</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.10.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">Ours</span></th>
<td id="S4.T4.10.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">1.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">0.4</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.10.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">36.3</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.10.10.6" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;"><span id="S4.T4.10.10.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">0.0</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt-level jailbreaks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although DDO targets mechanistic refusal removal, we also evaluate it against prompt-level attacks that operate purely at the input level (Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Compile-mode selection. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). DDO + debiasing achieves <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> GCG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> ASR, matching the best trained defenses, and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> on HumanJailbreaks. A plausible explanation is that optimization-based prompt attacks like GCG suppress the same low-dimensional refusal feature targeted by RFA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>; DDO’s decoy neurons partially re-inject refusal-correlated signal, making it harder for gradient-based prompt optimization to fully suppress refusal. However, semantic attacks like PAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="36.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>36.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">36.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR) circumvent refusal through meaning rather than activation geometry, and DDO provides no advantage here. Defending against semantic jailbreaks requires complementary input-level defenses such as input classifiers.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Ablations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Loss components. ‣ 4.3 Ablations ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> isolates each DDO component on Llama-3-8B-Instruct by removing one element at a time from the full configuration. All ablations preserve MMLU within 3 points of the base model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of gradient optimization.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Random orthogonal decoys (no optimization) achieve <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="72.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>72.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">72.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR—only a modest reduction from the undefended base (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85.1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85.1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85.1\%</annotation></semantics></math>). In contrast, gradient optimization under the full 4-part objective reduces ASR to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.8\%</annotation></semantics></math>, confirming that orthogonality alone is insufficient: decoys must be optimized to dominate the harmful–safe contrast that the attacker re-estimates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Loss components.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">confusion loss</em> <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{confusion}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>confusion</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{confusion}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusal-score loss</em> <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{refusal-score}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>refusal-score</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{refusal-score}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the most critical terms: removing either increases ASR to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="43.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>43.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">43.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="41.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>41.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">41.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. The confusion loss directly optimizes decoy directions to mislead the DIM estimator, while the refusal-score loss prevents first-token collapse (“Sure …” followed by refusal). The retain KL term stabilizes optimization (ASR <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="22.4\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>22.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">22.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> without it) but is less critical on its own.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>DDO ablation on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. RFA ASR = mean of 4 variants, 3-judge avg (%). <span id="S4.T5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">best</span> / <span id="S4.T5.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#C8E6C9;">good</span> / <span id="S4.T5.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFCDD2;">poor</span> / <span id="S4.T5.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E3F2FD;">ours</span>. All components contribute; confusion and refusal-score losses are most critical.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Neuron selection and compile mode.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Low-norm neuron selection outperforms random neuron choice (ASR <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>15.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>), supporting our design choice to edit low-impact units to reduce utility disruption while maintaining decoy strength. On Llama-3, replace mode outperforms additive (ASR <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16.5\%</annotation></semantics></math>), but this preference is model-specific (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS4" title="F.4 Compile Mode Selection Details ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.4</span></a>). Finally, layer placement upstream of the causal refusal zone is critical on models with localized refusal (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS5" title="F.5 Layer Placement Analysis ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Alternative defense mechanisms.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated 14 additional post-hoc mechanisms beyond DDO (Appendix Table <a href="#A6.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ F.12 Cross-Model Mechanism Comparison and Negative Results ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>). Linear defenses are brittle under re-estimation: Decoy Shear Transform (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="92\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>92</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">92\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR), Refusal Direction Rotation (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="68\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>68</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">68\%</annotation></semantics></math>), and Representation Rerouting (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="86\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>86</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">86\%</annotation></semantics></math>) are all defeated once the attacker recomputes DIM on the defended checkpoint. Aggressive edits (e.g., LM-Head Row Scaling) can drive RFA ASR near zero but at catastrophic utility cost (XSTest <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\%</annotation></semantics></math>, MT-Bench <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.72" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.72</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.72</annotation></semantics></math>). Finally, spreading decoy energy across more directions involves a tradeoff predicted by Corollary <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 3 (Optimal spectrum under an energy constraint). ‣ Decoy energy allocation. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>: diversified readers weaken rank-1 protection (ASR rises from 10% to 27% as the number of decoy groups <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> increases from 1 to 4) but strengthen higher-rank robustness (rank-16 ASR drops from 5% to 2%). The optimal <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> depends on the expected attacker rank budget (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Empirical Spectral Analysis ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proofs and Formalizations ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-architecture mechanism comparison.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated 8 post-hoc mechanisms across all 7 models (10–30 Optuna trials each; Appendix <a href="#A6.SS12" title="F.12 Cross-Model Mechanism Comparison and Negative Results ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.12</span></a>). DDO is the only single mechanism that achieves <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;10\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR reliably across all architectures. Other mechanisms are individually weak (e.g., gate_boost: <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="56\text{--}81\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>56</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>81</mn></mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">56\text{--}81\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR) or break generation on most models (diverse Q-head routing, rotation, V-projection, head amplification, and KV strengthening all fail the coherence check on Yi, Gemma-2, and GLM-4). Even random orthogonal decoys without gradient optimization fail on 5 of 7 models (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\text{--}53\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>53</mn></mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\text{--}53\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR). This supports the core DDO design: nonlinear SwiGLU gating plus gradient optimization (and per-model compile-mode selection) are jointly necessary for cross-architecture robustness. Full mechanism definitions are in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 All Mechanism Definitions ‣ Appendix D Additional Method Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Discussion</h3>

<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The role of nonlinearity.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Adaptive multi-phase RFA repeatedly estimates a linear DIM direction on the defended checkpoint. DDO’s SwiGLU gate makes the decoy response depend on the prompt: writing <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\mathrel{\triangleq}\langle\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\mathrel{\triangleq}\langle\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\ell},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>, the decoy amplitude scales as <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{silu}(\beta a)\cdot a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>silu</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{silu}(\beta a)\cdot a</annotation></semantics></math> and behaves like <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta a^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta a^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> for large positive <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>. The prompt-dependent decoy response can bias the DIM estimate toward the decoy subspace. Theorems <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1 (Subspace overlap bound). ‣ Spectral analysis of contrastive ablation. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2 (Overlap bound under orthogonal decoys). ‣ Decoy contrast decomposition. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> characterize the resulting subspace overlap under their stated assumptions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Resistance to DDO undo attacks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A defense-aware attacker may try to <em id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">undo</em> DDO by identifying edited neurons. Let <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>clean</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the reference refusal direction and <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>atk</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}</annotation></semantics></math> the DIM direction the attacker estimates on the defended checkpoint. The attacker scores each MLP gate row by <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}\mathrel{\triangleq}|\langle\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate}}^{(i)},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}\rangle|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐰</mi><mi>gate</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>atk</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}\mathrel{\triangleq}|\langle\mathbf{w}_{\mathrm{gate}}^{(i)},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}\rangle|</annotation></semantics></math> and zeros the down-projection columns corresponding to the highest-scoring rows. This would work if <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}\approx\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>atk</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>clean</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}\approx\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}</annotation></semantics></math>, since DDO writes <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>clean</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}</annotation></semantics></math>-aligned triggers into gate rows. Instead, estimator corruption rotates <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>atk</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}}</annotation></semantics></math> away from <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>clean</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}}</annotation></semantics></math>, so edited neurons are not salient under this score. Across Qwen3, Mistral-7B, and Yi, mid-zone target layers satisfy <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{cossim}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}})\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>cossim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>clean</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐝</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>atk</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{cossim}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{\mathrm{clean}},\hat{\mathbf{d}}_{\mathrm{atk}})\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math> and the modified rows’ scores fall within the natural top-5 distribution. The evaluated undo heuristics provide partial recovery, with ASR remaining below the undefended model in Table <a href="#A6.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ Post-attack ASR under undo heuristics. ‣ F.16 DDO Undo Attack Analysis ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS16" title="F.16 DDO Undo Attack Analysis ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.16</span></a>). ASR ranges from 6% to 12% without a sustained increase as the attacker’s probe budget grows from 32 to 1024 prompts per class (Appendix <a href="#A6.SS18" title="F.18 Probe-Budget Sensitivity ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.18</span></a>). Under rank-<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> SVD attacks, DDO with a single reader is effective at rank 1 (4% ASR) but degrades at higher ranks (39% at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k{=}16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k{=}16</annotation></semantics></math>; Appendix <a href="#A6.SS17" title="F.17 Rank-𝑘 Attack Sweep ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.17</span></a>). Diversifying readers across <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> groups extends higher-rank protection at the cost of rank-1 strength, as predicted by Corollary <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Corollary 3 (Optimal spectrum under an energy constraint). ‣ Decoy energy allocation. ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Empirical Spectral Analysis ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proofs and Formalizations ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison with trained defenses.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On standard RFA, DDO matches the strongest trained baselines across five model families (Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Cross-model generalization and baseline comparison. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower cost per configuration. Under Heretic on Llama-3, DDO alone (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\%</annotation></semantics></math>) remains weaker than RepBend <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> (<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.3\%</annotation></semantics></math>). A plausible explanation is <em id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">entanglement</em>: gradient-based training can distribute refusal across many parameters jointly, while closed-form edits are easier to localize and therefore easier to target with weight-level attacks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Limitations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing defenses against refusal ablation require gradient-based training per checkpoint, creating a bottleneck for the open-weight release cycle. DDO demonstrates that a mechanistic alternative—repurposing MLP neurons to corrupt the attacker’s contrastive estimator—can match trained baselines on standard RFA across six model families at <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="30\text{--}450\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>450</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{--}450\times</annotation></semantics></math> lower cost per configuration. The key insight is that contrastive attacks are only as good as the contrast they estimate: by injecting a large, harmful-selective, refusal-orthogonal decoy signal, DDO forces the attacker to ablate decoys rather than genuine refusal. 
<br class="ltx_break">DDO requires only a small generic probe set (128 harmful + 128 safe prompts), gradient optimization of the decoy parameters (base weights frozen, so memory overhead beyond inference is minimal), and a single GPU—no full finetuning infrastructure, no method-specific safety datasets, and few design decisions beyond compile mode and layer range. This makes it applicable by any party with access to the weights: model providers before release, downstream deployers, safety auditors, or automated agents. The feedback loop is fast (minutes per optimization run) and defense strength is controllable via compile mode and scalar gains (<math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta,s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta,s</annotation></semantics></math>), making DDO well-suited to agent-driven safety pipelines that iteratively harden and evaluate checkpoints.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations and future work.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DDO improves resistance to refusal ablation, but sustained adaptive re-estimation remains a challenge for all evaluated defenses. DDO can also increase over-refusal on some models, although orthogonal debiasing and compile-mode selection mitigate this effect (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Limitations and Future Work ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>). Future work could investigate post-hoc edits that distribute refusal behavior more broadly across parameters to improve robustness to weight-level attacks. Evaluating DDO alongside inference-time guardrails, such as Llama Guard, would help establish whether these approaches provide complementary protection.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

</section>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation covers three attack tiers and compares DDO with trained baselines across six primary model families, including six trained defenses on Llama-3. We also evaluate DDO alone on seven additional models. These experiments identify several limitations and directions for further study.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Adaptive attackers.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All defenses in Table <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Attack cost model. ‣ F.10 Adaptive Attack: Exact ASR and MT-Bench by Phase ‣ Appendix F Full Experimental Details ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> reach high ASR under sustained re-estimation within the eight-phase budget. DDO (rank <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>) reaches a worst-case ASR of <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>65</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65\%</annotation></semantics></math> (LlamaGuard-2), compared with <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="58\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>58</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">58\%</annotation></semantics></math> for RepBend. Evaluations with longer phase budgets, joint multi-direction projections, and estimators beyond DIM would help establish how robustness changes under stronger adaptive attacks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Weight-level attacks.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DDO achieves <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="18\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>18</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">18\%</annotation></semantics></math> ASR under Heretic on Llama-3, compared with <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="24.0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>24.0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">24.0\%</annotation></semantics></math> for Circuit Breakers, <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="82.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>82.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">82.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> for LAT, and <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="85.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>85.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">85.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> for ReFAT (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Standard RFA and Heretic on Llama-3. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). RepBend <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> achieves a lower ASR of <math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.3\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.3\%</annotation></semantics></math> through gradient-based parameter–behavior entanglement that is difficult to replicate with post-hoc edits alone. Closing this gap—e.g., via post-hoc edits that induce deeper entanglement surviving weight-level optimization—is a promising direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Over-refusal on some models.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DDO can reduce compliance with benign requests on some models. Similar or larger reductions occur with trained defenses, including LAT and ReFAT on Llama-3 (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Standard RFA and Heretic on Llama-3. ‣ 4.2 Results ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), indicating that over-refusal is a broader challenge for safety hardening. Orthogonal debiasing can restore benign compliance while preserving RFA robustness (Section <a href="#S3.SS0.SSS0.Px9" title="Orthogonal debiasing (utility repair). ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), and additive compilation reduces over-refusal on some architectures. Further work should investigate how to select these mitigations automatically for each model.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compile mode selection.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Choosing between replace and additive compilation currently requires evaluating both modes and comparing ASR and XSTest scores. This search is inexpensive relative to baseline finetuning, but a predictive rule based on properties such as refusal redundancy could reduce the need for repeated evaluations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Broader Impacts</h3>

<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Misuse of open-weight models.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training-free refusal removal has moved well beyond academic proof-of-concept. The mechanistic result that refusal is mediated by a low-dimensional residual-stream direction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> was rapidly operationalized into public tooling: community tutorials describe one-command uncensoring without retraining <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, and automated tools such as Heretic apply hyperparameter-optimized weight edits on a consumer GPU with no ML expertise required <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. A recent large-scale audit of public model repositories found over 8,600 safety-modified open-weight checkpoints across 1,300 namespaces, with more than half packaged in GGUF format optimized for local consumer-hardware deployment and accumulating tens of millions of tracked downloads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. Refusal removal has therefore become a distribution and hosting problem: users can either run abliteration scripts themselves, or simply download an already-modified checkpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Deployment considerations.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This distribution surface is exactly where DDO intervenes. Once aligned weights are publicly downloadable, there is no practical way to guarantee that all copies receive safety updates or can be rolled back <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>. Per-checkpoint safety retraining cannot address this at scale: it is too slow and too expensive to apply to every community finetune, merge, or re-quantized derivative hosted on a platform. DDO—requiring approximately two minutes per optimization run on a single GPU without base-model finetuning—can be applied by any party in the distribution chain before serving or redistributing a checkpoint. This is consistent with emerging policy guidance: NIST explicitly assigns monitoring and mitigation responsibilities to model-hosting platforms and other distribution channels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>. By raising the cost of the most accessible refusal-removal workflows, DDO addresses a gap that neither upstream safety training nor downstream prompt filtering can close alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Misuse domains.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The impact of increasing the attacker’s cost is largest in domains where compliant local assistance lowers barriers to serious misuse. For CBRN and biosecurity, LLM access has been shown to substantially accelerate novices on dual-use biology tasks: a controlled uplift study found that participants with LLM assistance were <math id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4.16\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.16\times</annotation></semantics></math> more accurate than internet-only controls, with 89.6% reporting little difficulty obtaining dual-use information despite safeguards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. Pre-deployment evaluation of high-consequence biological capabilities is now considered a baseline safety requirement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, and WMDP provides a systematic benchmark for hazardous biosecurity and chemical knowledge in LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>. For child safety, robust refusal reduces the availability of uncensored local assistants that can be used to facilitate grooming, coercion, or integration into abuse pipelines. Academic analysis identifies AI-generated CSAM as enabling revictimization, normalization, and lowered barriers to offending <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, while operational reporting documents sharply rising volumes and calls for safety-by-design action by platform providers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>. In both domains, DDO does not provide complete protection—determined adversaries with sufficient resources can still bypass it—but it raises the cost of the most accessible and widespread attack workflows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Potential negative impacts and dual-use concerns.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Three dual-use risks merit discussion. First, our adaptive multi-phase RFA attack is a new, stronger variant of existing RFA; however, it is a natural extension of publicly available methods, and we believe the defensive contribution outweighs this incremental offensive capability. Second, our mechanistic analysis of why defenses fail (nonlinearity requirements, subspace overlap bounds, neuron detectability) could inform adversaries seeking to circumvent safety measures; our analysis and released evaluation code are intended to support defensive design and robustness assessment. Third, DDO should be understood as a cost-raising hardening layer—not a complete safety guarantee—and we report its residual attack surfaces transparently in Section <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Limitations and Future Work ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Responsible disclosure.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We release DDO as a defensive hardening tool, together with code for evaluating its robustness to refusal-removal attacks. We do not release new uncensored model checkpoints or finetuning recipes for removing safety guardrails. All evaluation uses established public benchmarks (JailbreakBench, HarmBench, AdvBench) and models derived from publicly available instruction-tuned checkpoints.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Extended Related Work</h2>

<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mechanistic refusal representations and abliteration.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several analyses of RLHF-aligned LLMs show that refusal can be removed by ablating low-dimensional residual-stream features. Projecting out a rank-1 difference-in-means (DIM) direction—the <em id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">refusal feature</em>—often eliminates refusal, enabling Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA) and “abliteration” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. Such direction-based interventions have been contextualized under the Linear Representation Hypothesis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. Subsequent work argues that refusal geometry can be multi-dimensional (e.g., <em id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">concept cones</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> and multiple refusal-mediating directions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>), with orthogonal safety dimensions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> and evidence that harmfulness and refusal are encoded separately <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Complementary mechanistic studies localize safety-relevant structure to specific neurons <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite> and intermediate hidden states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, while sparse autoencoders reveal refusal as a composition of fine-grained latent features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al. [54]</a></cite> show that safety finetuning induces narrow, localized internal changes, which helps explain why contrastive estimators like RFA can locate and remove the refusal mechanism—motivating defenses that corrupt the estimator itself. We include both single-phase RFA and adaptive multi-phase RFA in our attack ladder (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Threat Model and Attacks ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Defenses against refusal ablation.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Existing defenses against RFA are largely training-time interventions. Circuit Breakers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> finetunes checkpoints with a representation-rerouting objective; LAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, targeted LAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, and ReFAT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> rely on adversarial finetuning; and representation-reshaping approaches such as RepBend <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and contrastive objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> modify refusal geometry during gradient-based training. A concurrent defense targets abliteration directly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, but still requires finetuning. While effective, these approaches require per-checkpoint training runs and, depending on the method, additional data collection or attack pipelines (e.g., adversarial examples) and hyperparameter tuning. In contrast, we study <em id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-hoc mechanistic weight editing</em>: decoy parameters optimized using a small prompt set and compiled into model weights with no architectural or runtime overhead, enabling rapid hardening and composition across open-weight releases.
Because these edits target specific components (layers, matrices, neurons), they also provide an interpretable and automatable complement to training-based hardening. Hyperparameter search with Optuna selects the configuration of these edits, which can also serve as an initialization for subsequent finetuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Prompt-level jailbreaks and robust refusal.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">LLMs are also vulnerable to prompt-based jailbreaks that circumvent refusal by optimizing adversarial inputs, without modifying model weights. We report three widely used automated attacks—GCG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, PAIR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, and AutoDAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>—under HarmBench’s standardized robust-refusal evaluation setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. ReFAT provides evidence that many prompt jailbreaks can suppress a low-dimensional residual-stream refusal feature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, linking these input-space attacks to the same refusal representation exploited by RFA; we therefore include them as a complementary evaluation of how our post-hoc weight edits affect robustness under input-space attack.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Over-refusal calibration.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Over-refusal—where aligned models refuse benign requests—has been studied through dedicated benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> and addressed via representation-level interventions. A single learned direction can calibrate false refusal in a training-free manner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, while targeted representation finetuning can shift refusal boundaries with minimal utility loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Our orthogonal debiasing mechanism (Section <a href="#S3.SS0.SSS0.Px9" title="Orthogonal debiasing (utility repair). ‣ 3 Method: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) ‣ Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) is complementary: it projects out an over-refusal direction from weight matrices after DDO, restoring benign compliance while preserving robustness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Real-world prevalence of abliteration.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The refusal direction exploited by RFA transfers across languages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, broadening the scope of the vulnerability beyond English-only settings. A large-scale audit found over 8,600 uncensored model repositories on HuggingFace, with abliterated variants achieving <math id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}74\text{--}80\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>74</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>–</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}74\text{--}80\%</annotation></semantics></math> compliance on unsafe prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. The growing ecosystem of automated abliteration tools across architectures has been surveyed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, and cheap post-hoc weight editing has been argued to pose serious safety risks for open-weight releases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>. These considerations motivate our focus on post-hoc hardening primitives that can be applied rapidly across checkpoints.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Notation and Background</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a standard decoder-only transformer architecture (e.g., Llama-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>). For a fixed token position (we omit token indices), let <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the residual-stream state at the input of layer <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> (hidden dimension <math id="A3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>). Each layer is <em id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">pre-norm</em>: RMSNorm is applied before attention and before the MLP, and each sublayer update is added back to the residual stream. We write RMSNorm with gain <math id="A3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝜸</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="A3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x})\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathbf{x}/\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{x})\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>RMSNorm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>RMS</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><msub><mi>𝜸</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{x})\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathbf{x}/\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{x})\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{x})\mathrel{\triangleq}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{2}+\varepsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>RMS</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>d</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{x})\mathrel{\triangleq}\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_{i}^{2}+\varepsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Attention.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>RMSNorm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell})</annotation></semantics></math>. Multi-head attention computes queries, keys, and values via learned projections:</p>

</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MLP (SwiGLU).</h4>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>RMSNorm</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>attn</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\ell}\mathrel{\triangleq}\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{h}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{attn}})</annotation></semantics></math>. Many modern LLMs (including Llama-3) use a SwiGLU MLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite> with gate/up projections <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{inter}}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>gate</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>up</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>inter</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{gate}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{inter}}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> and down projection <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{inter}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>down</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>inter</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{inter}}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A3.E8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="A3.E8X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
